inline.s: Cai Baozhong, a native of Suzhou, had lived for generations on Xueshi Street within the old city. In his early years he was a worker in a hardware shop in Shanghai, and later returned to Suzhou to serve as a clerk at a charitable institution. Though his family was poor, he could be content in poverty and devoted to the Way, being honest and simple, with a generous and kind heart. As a child he was already vegetarian, and as he grew older he loved to recite sutras. He took refuge in the Three Jewels and applied himself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation. Above all he delighted in revering and chanting the Avatamsaka Sutra, reciting several fascicles each day as a standing practice. Whenever the Lotus Society established an Avatamsaka Dharma assembly, he would resolve to take part, and he led the congregation, chanting correctly and with extraordinary reverence. Before the Cultural Revolution he once went to the Wuyin Hermitage at Tianping to leave home, taking Master Huihai as his teacher and receiving his inheritance of the robe and bowl. Before long, however, because circumstances would not allow it and his family dissuaded him, he could not fulfill his wish and so returned to lay clothes. Later, when his son was sent down to the Dafeng state farm in northern Jiangsu to settle, he went to live with him. Even at the grand age of seventy he still delighted in taking part in labor. In daily life he never gave up his practice, reciting and chanting as always. Half a year before his passing he felt a slight illness. On the day of his passing his right mindfulness was clear and distinct; hearing the sound of music in the air, he urgently called his family and said, 'The heavenly music is exquisitely beautiful; do you not hear it?' His family opened the door and went out to listen, and indeed heard the music ringing out in the sky. When they returned to the room, Baozhong had already entered stillness.

Elder Xu, the father of the layman Xu Zuyao, lived at No. 22 Zhujia Lane in Ningbo. Zuyao taught at Shanghai Jiao Tong University. The elder took refuge under Master Yinguang and diligently cultivated the Pure Land path. All day he wore the dark monastic robe, staying alone in the Buddha hall and single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name. Before his passing he showed a slight illness. His daughter asked him, 'Is there truly such a thing as rebirth in the Pure Land?' The elder answered, 'Just wait and see.' Having spoken, he sat cross-legged and recited the Buddha's name as before. After a moment the sound of recitation was no longer heard. When they looked at him, he had already passed away sitting. After his death a rare fragrance filled the room. His two sons and one daughter, witnessing these auspicious signs, also kept long-term vegetarianism and Buddha-recitation, and none of them ever married.

Shao Hui'an, originally named Zhi'an, at first believed in a heterodox teaching. Only after reading Master Yinguang's Collected Sayings did he come to believe deeply in the Three Jewels. He took refuge under Master Yin, turned single-mindedly to the Buddha, and diligently cultivated the Pure Land path. One year, because of a careless fall from a carriage, he hurt his qi and his strength daily declined. After more than a hundred days, his illness somewhat abated. On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth lunar month that year, when the abbot of Zhanggong Hall in his county, the monk Zixun, was cremated, he walked over to observe the ceremony and took part in the Buddha-recitation, his spirits as usual. On the way back he caught a chill, took to bed, and could not rise. From then on he recited the Buddha's name all the more earnestly, resolving to seek rebirth. By the twelfth day of the tenth month, knowing his time had come, he bade his family recite on his behalf. At the first watch of the night he asked his family, 'What time is it now?' His family answered falsely, 'The night is nearly spent.' Hui'an said, 'I shall depart westward at the chou hour tonight.' Having spoken, he resumed recitation. At the chou hour he said again, 'Amitabha Buddha and all the holy assembly are now before me; the Dharma Master Zixun has also come to welcome me. I am going.' Then, reciting 'Namo Amitabha Buddha' three times in a loud voice, he passed away auspiciously. His face was as in life and his limbs supple. After more than eight hours, when they examined him, his body had gone wholly cold, but the crown of his head remained warm.

Chen Lijun, a native of Tiantai, Zhejiang, was the fourth son of the layman Chen Fuchu, a family that had venerated the Buddha for generations. In childhood Lijun fell ill with consumption. One night, when the whole family had gone to bed, they suddenly heard Lijun cry out in alarm, 'How dreadful! How dreadful!' They hurried to his bedside and saw sweat streaming down his forehead and a look of great terror. When they asked the reason, Lijun said, 'There are several men holding clubs and ropes who want to bind me and carry me off.' His mother, knowing that this was the appearance of a ghostly realm, told him, 'The Bodhisattva can save you. Recite quickly “Namo Maha-Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva.”' Hearing this, Lijun earnestly invoked the holy name of the Great Being, and his family recited alongside him in support. Before long he said joyfully, 'They have all gone; I am no longer afraid.' He continued to hold the holy name. Suddenly he said to his family, 'Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva has come! The Bodhisattva shone a light on me and said to me, “I will take you along.”' His mother encouraged him, 'If you go with the Bodhisattva to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, that will be well.' Together they recited the holy name without pause. After a long while, Lijun's voice gradually faded, and he passed away. This was on the eighteenth day of the sixth month of 1943, when he was only fifteen.

Jiao Xunjian, the second son of Jiao Yuting of Shanghai, passed away in 1950 at only thirteen, and his auspicious signs were so manifest that he might well be called rare. As a child Xunjian was extremely clever but frail and often ill. When he was six, a monk passing by his gate turned and said to his mother, 'Your second son, who was born in the year of the ox, is the reincarnation of a monk who sat in retreat at Putuo. After three years in retreat he passed away, and following a deluded thought he entered the womb to become your son.' His mother at once had him take refuge, giving him the Dharma name Peixin. Because his karmic roots were deeply planted, he knew to recite the Buddha's name even as a little child; every night before sleeping he would hold the holy name without ceasing. In daily life he urged his mother to give alms. The money she gave him for sweets he never spent recklessly, but gathered it into sums and donated them. By nine, his frame grew daily thinner; a doctor found that his thigh bone had been injured and that it had developed into bone tuberculosis. After treatment he lay in bed for three years before recovering. To be throughly safe, the doctor advised a bone-setting operation to prevent a recurrence, so he entered the Zhongmei Hospital and set about convalescing. While hospitalized, whenever he met a fellow patient in the same room who needed an operation, he would urge him not to be timid but to recite the name of Amitabha Buddha single-mindedly, and his pain would subside. When the operation was to be performed on him, a day beforehand he shaved his head, bathed, cut his nails, and rinsed his mouth. When all this was done, he insisted on having his photograph taken and asked for a brush to inscribe a poem. His family would not allow it, saying there was no need to be hasty about the photograph and that the poem could wait for another day. Xunjian suddenly spoke with a stern face, 'Now both within and without my body shines transparent. How pitiable that your flesh and blood have covered your minds, so that even with Buddhas and Bodhisattvas before your very eyes you cannot recognize them.' Again facing the mirror he said, 'My two ears have, in these days, grown as large as a Bodhisattva's.' His family rebuked him for speaking wildly, but he only smiled and said nothing. His mother happened to be ill at home, and Xunjian thought of her daily, saying, 'How is Mother's illness? Can she come tomorrow? I have written an inscription in the Diamond Sutra; it is not to be looked at now, but in two days it may be sent for Mother to read.' For while Xunjian was in hospital, his mother had placed a copy of the Diamond Sutra at his pillow. The next day the operation was finished and he was clear-headed. Before long, however, a sudden change came over him and all remedies failed. The time drew on to the seventh hour and he passed away. When his family came to look, his face wore a smile; the next day, at the encoffining, the crown of his head was still warm.

Liu Xintong was a son of the Liu family of Kaifeng, Henan. His ancestral home was in Shanxi, and he had come to Bian with his father, an official traveling on duty. At thirteen he suddenly developed scrofulous swellings on his neck, with pus and blood oozing forth, a stench too foul to approach, and every kind of pain. He lay in bed unable to rise, and for a whole year did not recover, weeping day and night as he sat awaiting death. His father was on official duty in another province, while his mother remained at home to look after him. One day the boy saw his mother change her clothes and go out, and asked, 'Where are you going?' She replied, 'To pay respects to a master.' He asked, 'What is the use of paying respects to a master?' She said, 'To recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West, to escape the sea of suffering of the Saha world.' The boy earnestly begged to go in her place. His mother then, on his behalf, took refuge under the Dharma Master Mingde and received the Eight Precepts of the one-day fast. When she returned home, she saw the boy kneeling upright with palms joined, motionless, as if he had no illness, and she was overjoyed. For the boy had been confined to his bedding, unable to turn for months. From then on he devoutly recited the Buddha's name without ceasing. After about three months he said to his mother, 'My karmic hindrances are exhausted. I am about to be reborn in the West. That Mother should be burdened for my sake is also bitter. Please invite people who recite the Buddha's name to come and help.' His mother invited several fellow practitioners to come to the house and recite on his behalf. At first, because the bedroom was foul, they did so outside. Before long they suddenly noticed a rare fragrance in the room, its scent rich and powerful, not like the aloes and sandalwood of this world. The group at once went in to look, and there was Xintong seated upright, palms joined, eyes closed, reciting the Buddha's name. In an instant he passed away. The rare fragrance lingered three days without dispersing.

Zhang Yiliu, named Yuan, styled Disan, and taking Yiliu as his late sobriquet, was a native of Jingjiang County, Jiangsu, who lived at No. 25 Jintaishi Lane in Suzhou. In his youth he studied in Japan, and after returning home he devoted himself to the cause of education, later taking refuge under Master Yinguang. The layman excelled at poetry and played the qin well, and the family treasured more than ten antique qin. His poetry was plain and serene, much resembling that of Bai Juyi. In his later years he declined all worldly dealings and devoted himself solely to the Pure Land path. Once his eyes became diseased and he lost his sight; a hundred physicians had no effect. He therefore set aside all medicine and single-mindedly recited the Buddha's name. In only a few months his sight returned, and he could read sutras and write as before. He took as his sole principle the recollection of Amitabha through pointing to a direction and establishing a form, and he did not delight in abstruse talk. Before his death he himself composed several verses on Buddha-recitation, one of which ran, 'I came without a single thread; now I go with no thread as well. Liberation is to be found in a single thought, and that thought is fixed ever on the name.' Soon after he showed a slight illness and passed away in peace. At his cremation he left a great many multicolored relic flowers; this was in 1947. Among his writings were the Discourse on the Grand Outline of the Pure Land, Epistemology of the West, Tuosha's Pure Land Essays, the Verses of the Xiuren Hall, the Random Jottings of the Xiuren Hall, and the Record of Mount Lingyan, all printed and circulated by the Honghua Society. The History of Chinese Agriculture and the Selected Pastoral Poems were works of his earlier years. He also translated a number of Japanese works on the Pure Land, which were never published.

Dou Cunwo, a native of Pizhou, Jiangsu, was once rich, but being no good at managing his livelihood his family gradually declined. In his later years he was quite poor, yet he remained unconcerned about it. He was of a generous and honest nature, and even when cheated to his face he would not contend. In his early years he firmly believed in the teachings of Cheng and Zhu and had even slandered Buddhism. A fellow townsman, Liu Renhang, urged him to read the Awakening of Faith, whereupon he resolved to take refuge in Buddhism. In Shanghai, at the seat of Master Yinguang, he received the Pure Land teaching, read and chanted the Mahayana, and encouraged others to cultivate the Pure Land path. In 1945 Pizhou suffered a great flood, and together with Hu Songnian he initiated relief efforts, calling the benefactors of Shanghai to gather and jointly contribute funds. Le Huibin was the first to pledge one thousand yuan, and the other benefactors followed one by one. Yet when all the pledges were made, the sum was still not gathered. The layman then generously pledged ten thousand yuan to complete the task, and did so without attaching his name. His love of virtue and his generosity were all of this sort. Being frugal by nature, whenever his family wore something at all showy he would scold them. After Master Yinguang passed to the West, he organized with the Dharma Master Desen and others in Shanghai the Permanent Commemoration Society for Master Yinguang, and arranged the Honghua Monthly, taking the post of editor-in-chief himself. In its pages he published many articles promoting the Pure Land path, but none bore his real name, so that no one knew he was their author. In 1954 he joined with the Monk Miaozhen in compiling the Illustrated Biography of Master Yinguang, inviting well-known painters and calligraphers of Shanghai to create the paintings and calligraphy. At that time his finances were in extreme difficulty, so that he could not always get a meal, yet he still donated funds to set things going. The layman was deeply versed in doctrine and held pure views; his discussion of the Dharma was in all things founded on Master Yinguang. He once said, 'To fulfill one's human relationships and do one's part, to ward off evil and preserve sincerity, this is the stairway by which one becomes a Buddha; and to believe, vow, and recite the Buddha's name, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land — this is the destination of a myriad practices.' He also said, 'In studying Buddhism one should be like a Confucian scholar, intent on bettering the world and benefiting others, sharing the joys and sorrows of the age, and should not make one's own escape from birth and death the ultimate aim. When Bodhidharma said “in this land there are many with Mahayana capacities”, he was speaking of the Confucian school.' Near the end he showed a slight illness. On the day of his death, after a meal, Professor Shi Shoumo came to visit, and he still rose to eat and drink, chatting and laughing as usual. Toward evening, with a few yawns, he went inside to rest a while. After a long time he did not come out; when his family parted the curtain to look, he had already grown still. This was in November of 1965. He lived to eighty-one.

Xia Mianzun, in his early years, taught alongside Master Hongyi at the Zhejiang Women's Normal School. After Master Hongyi left home to become a monk, the layman too took refuge in the Three Jewels. At his deathbed, Chen Hailiang instructed him to recite the Amitabha Sutra; before he had finished the scroll he passed away. At his cremation he left a great many relic flowers.

Shen Yongjiu, named Shanchang, was a native of Sanbanqiao, Haiyan, Zhejiang. He lost his father at birth, and as a young man graduated from Fudan University in Shanghai. The layman served his widowed mother with the utmost filiality. He loved virtue and gave alms, bearing the manner of the virtuous ancients. He believed deeply in the Pure Land, advanced zealously in Buddha-recitation, and observed the precepts with utmost strictness. In 1912 he traveled to Hangzhou, made pilgrimage to Yunqi, and paid respects to the stupa of Master Lianchi. In summer he went again to Putuo to revere the Great Being Avalokiteshvara. When autumn came he suddenly fell ill. His family wished to send for treatment, but the layman firmly refused, saying, 'Life is like the morning dew, and living in the world is like a dream. This body of four elements was never mine to begin with; what need is there of medicine? Only single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name and, leaving far behind the dust of the world, behold Amitabha Buddha face to face; then my wish is fulfilled.' By the thirtieth day of the ninth month his illness had grown worse. Neighbors came to see him, and all, moved with gratitude, urged him to recite the Buddha's name. At that time men and women, old and young, and even the servants they employed, all received his teaching and recited the Buddha's name in chorus. The layman spurred himself all the more, single-minded upon Amitabha, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. At the moment of death he suddenly turned to those on either side and said, 'A five-colored lotus has now appeared before me.' Having spoken, he closed his eyes and passed away. His features were unchanged and a rare fragrance filled the room. He was only twenty-five years of age.

Ma Liao'an, named Yaoqing, was an outstanding student of the Qing attached to the government schools. A native of Pingchao Township, Nantong, Jiangsu, he was born in the first year of the Tongzhi reign. In the Republican era he abandoned the old custom of the civil examinations and took up modern learning, founding Shigang Primary School to teach people to read, with benefiting both self and others as his lifelong aspiration. He successively served as principal of Pingchao Primary School, chairman of the education association, and a school-inspection officer, working in education for several decades and tirelessly nurturing the young. The layman had seven sons; the fourth, named Lingyuan, taught at Nantong Normal School. From the school's principal, the layman Jiang Yiyuan, Lingyuan obtained Pure Land scriptures and brought them home for his father to read. The moment his father set eyes on them he rejoiced and praised them without end, and so turned his heart to the Western Pure Land, reciting the holy name several thousand times a day. In autumn 1926 he suddenly contracted a slight illness and recited the Buddha's name with even greater vigor, also chanting the Prajna Heart Sutra. On the twentieth day of the eleventh lunar month of 1927, he sat upright in proper posture, invoked Amitabha Buddha, and with a composed smile gave up his body to be reborn. His family knelt in a circle, all proclaiming the Buddha's name. After two hours they boiled pine boughs and sandalwood to make water to bathe the layman's body. His joints were supple as in life. Several hundred neighbors and villagers came to grieve, and respectfully honored him with the title of Master Xiao Jing. He lived to sixty-six.

Wang Xuzhao, styled Mingqiu, was a native of Dafan in Wuyuan County, Anhui. His family was poor for generations, and at forty he was still heavily in debt. After thirty years of diligent commerce he gradually became a well-to-do household. The layman lived frugally and would not waste a thing. After taking refuge in the Three Jewels he delighted in giving alms and undertaking good works. The ancestral halls and Buddhist temples of the village were all repaired at his own expense. The rugged footpaths within a dozen li of his home were all leveled into smooth roads. He relieved the orphaned and destitute and rescued the many from suffering, and he did his utmost in such good works as burying uncovered bones. He printed and distributed the Collected Works of Anshi, the Collected Essays of Master Yinguang, and all manner of wholesome books, so as widely to exhort the world. All the merit he did he dedicated in a written vow to rebirth in the West, wishing that he and all sentient beings might be reborn together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. In his daily practice the layman was extremely earnest. He venerated the golden Buddha image and held the six-syllable sacred name, morning and evening, in summer and winter, without a break. His feet once suffered from a rheumatic ailment, making walking difficult and kneeling painful; but because his Buddha-recitation was so sincere, before long he could kneel and recite and walk in circumambulation as usual. In 1930, the year of gengwu, when the layman was eighty-two, he said to the lotus friend Cao Yunxi, 'When I go to be reborn in the West, please come and help me recite the Buddha's name.' Ten days before his death he invited the layman Cao Yunxi to his home to help recite the holy name. When the ten days were complete, he was reborn as he had wished. After death his face wore a smile, his expression was as usual, the crown of his head warm and his body supple. His family heard the wooden fish and bell in the Buddha hall sound by themselves, and heavenly music rang in the air. An edict in his last will asked that during the forty-nine days the whole family remain vegetarian and recite the Buddha's name. His children and grandchildren all followed this.

Zheng Xibin, a native of Jimo, Shandong, was a merchant. Having read Buddhist sutras and learned of the benefit of Buddha-recitation, he resolved to recite the Buddha's name and never married. In 1933, in Qingdao, he received the Three Refuges from the Dharma Master Cixu. From then on his heart grew all the more sincere, and he handed all household affairs to his younger brother so that he could devote himself wholeheartedly to recitation. The layman was able to lecture on the Amitabha Sutra, and every year he would travel from Jimo, through Qingdao, to Pingdu County to expound it for fellow practitioners. In spring 1939 he again went to Pingdu to lecture. When the lecture was done and the crowd dispersed, he shared a meal with five or six fellow practitioners, and after the meal he suddenly said he wanted to rent a room. When his friends asked why, the layman said, 'I am about to be reborn, and I fear that dying in someone else's house would be inauspicious.' His friends said, 'We are old friends of many years' standing. Not to speak of being reborn in the Buddha-land; even if you lay bedridden and died in our homes, what would it matter? There are quite a few here who recite the Buddha's name. If you are truly certain, you can also serve as an example for the people of this district.' His friends thereupon prepared two rooms and set up a couch for him to rest. The layman at once climbed onto the couch, sat cross-legged facing west, and said to the assembled friends, 'I take leave of you all; I am going now. We have believed in the Buddha together this while, so please recite and see me on my way.' His friends asked him to speak a verse, but the layman said, 'There is no need for a verse. You see me in this state, coming and going freely. If you practice as I have, that will be a fine remembrance.' Having spoken, in less than a quarter of an hour, he passed away with a smile. His younger brother had at first not believed in the Buddha, and seeing his elder abandon the family estate to devote himself wholly to recitation, he had thoroughly disapproved. Only after repeated persuasion did he grudgingly believe and recite, though not earnestly. When he saw with his own eyes the layman recite the Buddha's name and pass away, knowing his time beforehand and coming and going freely, he at last understood the merit and benefit of Buddha-recitation, and so applied himself wholeheartedly and sincerely to the practice. Three years later he too knew his time and, reciting the Buddha's name, passed away.

Lan Zhongxian, named Daozheng, was a native of Huai'an, Jiangsu. In his youth he entered the county school and soon drew a government stipend. In adulthood he took up politics, holding important posts. In middle age, in the old capital, he was introduced by a friend into the Tongshen Society. Over time he came to know that what it transmitted was but fragments gathered from Buddhism and Daoism, fitted to its own ideas and set up as a school of its own. The books it compiled and printed indiscriminately cited the scriptures and treatises of the three religions, falsely claiming that they came from one source; they were diffuse and chaotic, with no true aim, and he knew in his heart that this was wrong. Later he obtained circulating copies of newly compiled introductory Buddhist books, and they suited him greatly. He then resolutely abandoned the false teaching, took refuge in the Three Jewels, received and kept the Five Precepts, and studied the Sanskrit scriptures intently. Nor did he neglect practice; he recited the liturgies, hymns and praises deeply until he was thoroughly at ease with every cadence. He then journeyed widely, consulting teachers everywhere, and came to know the one matter of stepping beyond. In 1935, when the Nanjing Buddhist Pure Karma Society was founded, he was elected a director. He led the members in chanting morning and evening, guiding them gradually and teaching tirelessly. He proposed that at the close of each month they perform the Great Compassion Repentance for three days and release life once, as a standing rule. Every summer he further held assemblies for the Avatamsaka and Ksitigarbha sutras, and the hall would be filled with those who joyfully joined. When the war of resistance broke out, his colleagues scattered and the society's work ceased. In 1939 he set aside a quiet room in his private house in Huai'an and established the Huai'an Buddhist Pure Karma Society. The next year he purchased a two-story building as the new quarters, opening a main hall of three bays enshrining the Three Sages of the West. Behind the hall were the abbot's quarters, and to the right he built a Ksitigarbha hall. The layman and his wife lived there together, cultivating the Pure Land path together. Though he had been tempered under the Chan school, his faith in the Pure Land teaching was deeper still, and he held Master Yinguang in the utmost reverence. His nature was stern and upright; in leading younger practitioners he allowed no laxity. On those whose faith was not earnest or whose conduct was not pure he would pour forth rebuke; if their chanting did not follow the liturgy he would at once correct it. In 1943 he had two coffins made to serve for the remains of himself and his wife. In autumn 1944 he handed the society's affairs over to others, and himself cultivated only the Pure Land, single-mindedly hastening west. At the beginning of the eleventh month of 1945 he wrote to a friend, 'Next year I shall be going.' The following year, on the sixteenth day of the sixth lunar month, at night he dreamed of entering a pure realm. The halls were lofty and deep, the buildings joined to the clouds, a white radiance shone as in daylight, and before the gate banners and canopies seemed to flutter. As he was gazing upward at it, he suddenly woke. He knew his time for rebirth had come. On the nineteenth, which happened to be the holy birthday of the Great Being Avalokiteshvara, he joined the members in chanting and reciting. On the twentieth, as soon as he finished his morning service, he felt faintly unwell, yet he spoke as in ordinary days, and, sitting upright reciting the Buddha's name, remained clear of mind. By two in the afternoon he formed the Buddha mudra, and the sound of recitation gradually grew faint, then grew still. When they looked, he had already passed away. The next morning at the encoffining the crown of his head was still warm, his face as in life, and his whole body supple. He was sixty-eight, and left no children.

Wang Jiren, a native of Rugao in northern Jiangsu, lived at the river mouth of Rugao, making his living by running a rice business and owning several boats in the shipping trade, so his family was quite well off. The layman was kind in his dealings, generous and broad-minded, and delighted in giving. He protected the Three Jewels, fearing only that he might do so less than fully. He and his wife both kept long-term vegetarianism. At festivals the whole family ate vegetarian; in ordinary times the family observed the ten vegetarian days each month without killing without cause. Around 1931 he went to Baoguo Temple in Suzhou to call on Master Yinguang and asked to take refuge. From then on his recitation and practice grew all the more zealous, and he often had his family join him in chanting. He had three sons and three daughters, all of them very obedient and filial. His eldest son and daughter-in-law in particular did their utmost in filiality, attending him all day long and never leaving his side. The layman was wont to instruct his children to study diligently, to be honest and dependable, to pity the poor, to revere the Three Jewels, and to accumulate virtue and do good, and not to store up wealth for their descendants, which would cause them to gain without labor and squander it. Under his teaching, though the family was many in number, they all lived in harmony and never once quarreled. In 1948, free of illness and pain, he peacefully gave up his body, and, reciting the Buddha's name, passed away. Three days before his passing he knew his time. Before death he shaved his head and bathed, put on clean clothes and over them the Dharma robe, and sat upright in the central hall, palms joined, reciting the Buddha's name like an aged bhikshu. Then he said to his family, 'I am going. Do not weep; it is the recitation of the Buddha's name that matters.' Having spoken he passed away, at seventy years of age.

Xiao Houzhai, named Peishen, was a native of Hangzhou, Zhejiang, and a descendant of the Xiao house of the Liang dynasty; he had long lived in Shanghai. He was born in 1883. He once went to study in Japan, and after returning home he taught at the Zhejiang Law College. The layman had deep karmic roots and firmly believed in the Buddha. His nature was kind and merciful; he kept long-term vegetarianism and often bought living creatures to release them. For eighteen years he practiced diligently, chanting sutras and revering the Buddha, without a moment's pause even in scorching summer or freezing winter. His demeanor was calm and dignified, with the bearing of an elder. Neighbors and relatives all spoke of him as a good man. At sixty-eight, that is in 1951, during the summer, he took out the various folding fans he had stored up over his life and aired them in the sun, saying to his children and grandchildren, 'These fans, after this autumn, will never be used again.' That same year, on the thirteenth day of the ninth lunar month, he passed away without illness. At death his right mindfulness was clear; facing west, lying in the auspicious posture, he recited the Buddha's name without ceasing. After his death his whole body was cold, but the crown of his head alone remained warm, and his limbs were supple as in life.

Liu Changxin was from Sunjiashan, Fufeng County, Shaanxi. In his early years he wandered onto a wrong path, and later, knowing it was not right, he went to the Dharma Master Liangqing at Famen Temple, asking to be led out of the maze and shown the path of awakening. The master, knowing his goodness, accepted him as a disciple, taught him the Pure Land way, and bade him believe, vow, and recite the Buddha's name in hope of rebirth in the Pure Land. Changxin rejoiced beyond measure, saying, 'Without climbing the summit, one does not know the height of Mount Tai; without gazing on the vast ocean, one cannot know the breadth of the sea. Now I know where to return.' From then on he cultivated the Pure Land path alone, practicing with untiring effort. He once said, 'Who is the deathless immortal who never grows old? Diligently recite the Buddha's name and cherish your remaining years. The melon's stem drops only after it ripens; the persimmon turns sweet only late in autumn.' In mid-twelfth month of 1955, Changxin went to Famen to take leave of Liangqing. He brought the clothes of his whole life and asked the master to give them to the people as a bond of connection, and he offered several silver dollars to the temple to make a halo for the Buddha image. After returning home he dug his own grave and made ready the funeral. At eight in the morning of the tenth day of the first month the following year, he changed his clothes and bathed, sat upright reciting the Buddha's name, and ended his life without illness. His ease and freedom of bearing were no different from in life. He died at eighty-three.

Luo Fengzhang was a native of Guichi, Anhui. He lost his father in swaddling clothes and was raised by his mother, who held to her widowhood, so the household's circumstances were meager. As a youth he studied with great determination. Once grown, he was introduced by a relative to a post at the Qixin Cement Company in Qingdao. He was sincere and honest in character, and was valued by his superiors, who transferred him to the Xinfu Printing and Dyeing Mill in Shanghai as deputy manager. Because he managed affairs well and was not careless toward money, he won the deep trust of those in charge. His nature was kind and merciful; he treasured blessings, pitied the poor, and hastened to help those in distress. During the war, while others hoarded goods to grow rich, he alone held to integrity and would never take money unjustly. He lived in a few humble rooms, depending on his salary to get by. He loved virtue and gave alms, often providing medicine and relieving the poor, and for a time served as chairman of the Red Cross. His second wife, Zhao, venerated the Three Jewels and often urged him to believe in the Buddha. At sixty he at last went to Lingyan and took refuge at the seat of the Dharma Master Desen. From then on he recited the Buddha's name and turned his heart to the Pure Land. At seventy-two he suddenly showed signs of illness. On the eighth day of the third lunar month of 1966 he passed away. As he departed, he lay on his back on the bed, palms joined at his chest, loudly reciting the holy name. His wife invited a good many fellow practitioners to recite on his behalf. From three in the morning until about nine, the layman suddenly turned to his wife and said, 'The room is filled with great light.' He went on, 'The Buddha has come! Golden light flashes brilliantly, and there are many, many Buddhas.' Having spoken, he recited the Buddha's name with single-minded devotion and spoke no more. Amid the sound of the group's recitation, his eyes slowly closed and he passed away in peace. After death his hands formed the Amitabha mudra upon his belly, and his face was as in life.

Yang Wenlin, a native of northern Jiangsu, lived on Qiujiang Road in Shanghai and had one son and three daughters. All his life he studied medicine and made it his profession. At thirty-eight, feeling the impermanence of the world, he first came to believe in the Buddha, gave up meat, and devoted himself solely to the Pure Land path. He once went to Putuo in Ningbo to take refuge under the Monk Wenzhi of Mount Foding, who gave him the Dharma name Huixiang. He lived on the mountain for three and a half years, listening to lectures on the Shurangama Sutra with considerable insight. After taking refuge in the Buddha, the layman strove in his practice with great zeal, earnestly reciting the Buddha's name without changing his subject, and so remained unvarying for forty or fifty years. In 1974 the layman was already eighty-five. The following winter he suddenly contracted cancer of the esophagus. For seventy-five days he felt no pain and recited the Buddha's name as before. A few days before his passing he knew his time, and said to people, 'I have already seen two youthful attendants come to lead me to rebirth in the West. It has been a week now; I cannot let them wait for me long, so I have chosen to be reborn on the twenty-third day of the first month.' His third daughter worked in a silk mill in Suzhou, and the twenty-third was the mill's day off. Later he suddenly said again, 'The day I chose is not very good. I have decided to move it three days earlier, and will pass away on the twentieth of the first month.' He bade his family telegraph his daughter in advance so that she would return the moment she received it. On the day of his passing he had his body wiped clean; when that was done it was already noon. He himself put on clean clothes and a long gown, tidied himself, and lay upon the bed, reciting the Buddha's name aloud. At three in the afternoon his daughter returned. He made a gesture for her to sit before the bed and recite the Buddha's name together with him. By seven in the evening his pulse gradually stopped, though his lips still moved slightly. Leaning down to look, they could still hear the faintest sound of Buddha-recitation. The whole family joined their palms and chanted the Buddha's name loudly, and amid the sound of the recitation the layman peacefully passed away. His whole body was cold, but the crown of his head alone was warm.

Jiang Chang'an, a native of Rugao, Jiangsu, lived in the northeastern countryside of Rugao, of lower-middle peasant stock, under the Nanling Commune. The layman was honest and sincere, content in poverty and devoted to the Way. He believed in the Buddha early, and sent his son to leave home at Dinghui Temple — the Master Dechun. At thirty-two he took refuge under the old Master Xuyun, who gave him the name Kuanren. His son later went to Zhenjiang to investigate. On one visit home to see his aged father he brought back a scroll of the Diamond Sutra. Seeing that his father was in poor health, he urged him to recite the Buddha's name and to hold to the Diamond Sutra. The moment the layman set eyes on the Diamond Sutra he received it as a treasure. From that resolve he chanted it three times a day, and for more than thirty years he did not miss a single day. In 1977, at a quarter to six in the afternoon of the nineteenth day of the first lunar month, free of pain and with right mindfulness clear, he recited the Buddha's name and passed away auspiciously. After death the crown of his head was warm and his limbs supple. He lived to ninety-one.

Jiang Wenrui, a native of the southern countryside of Yangzhou, lived in Zhabei, Shanghai. In his early years he had opened a shoe shop. He was upright and generous; whenever anyone was in difficulty he would do his utmost to help. He believed deeply in the Three Jewels, taking refuge under the old Master Yuanzhi of Nanjing. At thirty he resolved to keep long-term vegetarianism and recited the Buddha's name devoutly. The Zhabei Buddhist Laymen's Grove was founded by him, and he bore all its expenses. His heart was given to joyful giving, and he won the hearts of the people. During the Cultural Revolution, when reciting the Buddha's name was regarded as a reactionary act, the layman still recited the holy name aloud as before; his neighbors, knowing this, did not interfere. At seventy-nine, that is on the sixth day of the ninth lunar month of 1978, he passed away sitting without illness. One day before his passing, entrusted by a friend, he went about the whole day inviting fellow practitioners to perform a Buddhist service. After returning home he felt slightly unwell. That very evening he shaved his head, bathed, and changed into clean clothes, saying to his family, 'Let me rest a while; do not disturb me.' He then went to his room, closed his eyes, and sat quietly. Within no time at all, when his family entered the room to look, he had already passed away peacefully.

Tao Shide, whose Dharma name was Nengde, took refuge in 1947 under the old Master Longji, the twenty-fifth generation of the Linji lineage, and in 1954, at Ganlu Temple on Ma'anshan in Ningxia, received the lay bodhisattva precepts. From the time the layman took refuge in the Three Jewels, he practiced the ten-recitation method every day without a break. Later he also mastered the two daily liturgies, and in his daily chanting took a single phrase of the Buddha's name as his main practice, reciting the Five Pure Land Sutras, the Lotus Sutra, the Diamond Sutra, and other Mahayana scriptures as ancillary practice. In 1979 he fell into bodily suffering, yet he held to the Buddha's name with all the more zeal. He repeatedly instructed his family and kin, 'When I am dying, be sure not to follow the common custom of moving me about and weeping. Cremate the body and do not bury it.' On the sixteenth day of the third lunar month of 1981, eleven days before his passing, at noon he said to his family, 'You should prepare my funeral arrangements; I am about to go.' On the twenty-fourth, three days before death, his family invited the old Master Longyuan. The moment they met, he said only, 'In my heart there is only the Buddha; at death I will not be apart from the Buddha.' On the twenty-fifth he sat or lay at ease, calm and free, showing no sign of illness. At nine on the twenty-sixth, sitting upright facing west, he recited the Buddha's name and passed away. At that time the Dharma Master Longyuan and several dozen fellow practitioners were at his side. The next day his face was as in life, radiant and bright, and all who saw it could not but praise. On the fourth day he was cremated; his limbs were supple, and his ashes were of colored hue.

Shen Fukang lived in the countryside of Xiaoshan County, Zhejiang. He began eating vegetarian at fifty-two, received the Three Refuges from the old Master Lanting of Xiaoshan at fifty-five, and from sixty devoted himself solely to releasing life. Once he sold a house left by his ancestors for a thousand yuan and used it all to buy creatures to release. His children gave him a monthly allowance of twenty-five yuan for living expenses; apart from five or six yuan for rice, salt and small necessities, the rest he also used for releasing life. The layman had been prone to illness by nature, but after taking up vegetarianism and releasing life his strength grew sound, and for over twenty years he never sought a doctor or took medicine. From seventy-two he began solely to hold the Buddha's name, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. He said that even in his dreams he could continue to uphold the Name without ceasing. In 1982 the layman was seventy-four. Toward the end of that year he lay ill for more than ten days, his mind clear, without the slightest look of stupor. One day before his passing he said to others, 'I am going. If not today, then tomorrow.' He added, 'My heart is very joyful, without a trace of pain.' He bade his children recite on his behalf, and instructed them to sell the coffin he had prepared, using the proceeds to release life, and to have his body cremated in accord with Buddhist practice. His children hired a car to take him to Hangzhou, since Xiaoshan had no cremation facilities, and on the way, within the car, with palms joined, he passed away in peace. This was at four in the afternoon on the fourth of January 1983. Three hours after his death his whole body was cold, but the crown of his head was still warm. He was seventy-five. When the layman was sixty-five, one day he rode a bicycle carrying a large bag of snails to the Broken Bridge beside West Lake in Hangzhou to release them. When it was done he rode back to Xiaoshan. On the way a jeep came head on; his bicycle was knocked over and he fell to the ground. The jeep's front wheel rolled over his foot, leaving a clear mark. The driver at the sight was frightened and at a loss. The layman stood up wholly unharmed, gave a serene smile, made a deep bow, and went on his way.

Yang Qinfang, of Shenjiamen Township in Putuo County, Zhejiang, lived in the Xida neighborhood. Born in 1907, she passed away westward on the twenty-eighth of October 1983, aged seventy-seven. The laywoman did not at first believe in the Buddha. At seventy-five her son died suddenly of illness, and feeling the impermanence of life she resolved to take up vegetarianism and Buddha-recitation. Whenever she recited, her voice was so earnestly sincere that the neighbors could all hear it. From her first resolve until her passing, it had not yet been two full years. At the end of September 1983 she caught a cold, and on the fourth of October she took to bed. She saw a white lotus bud fall upon her chest. At the time, all her family smelled a rare fragrance filling the room, which took half a day to disperse. During her illness she was entirely free of pain. On the evening of the twenty-eighth of October, the twenty-fourth day of the ninth lunar month, she suddenly instructed her family, 'Quickly, help me recite the Buddha's name; I am going with Amitabha Buddha.' Her family asked, 'Do you see the Buddha?' She answered, 'Yes.' Thereupon she joined her palms and made the gesture of revering the Buddha. When her family proposed inviting pure companions to help recite, she stopped them, saying, 'Do not go calling on people in the night.' Then she said aloud, 'Make room; the Buddha is coming.' Next she traced her son's name with her finger. Her younger sister, who had long believed in the Buddha, seeing this, spoke solemnly to her, 'Your time of death has come; set your mind wholly on the West, and from this moment end birth and death. Let go of all ties; think of neither enemy nor kin. Only recite Amitabha Buddha and go with Amitabha Buddha, and do not be thinking of your son.' The laywoman nodded in assent. At that time several people in the room were reciting 'Namo Amitabha Buddha' in unison, and she silently followed the sound. Before long, with a smile, she passed away, at seven twenty in the evening. Twenty-four hours after her passing her whole body was supple, and the crown of her head was still warm.
